claim.pdf_says: Table 1 - COBOL character repertoire (Continued) | Basic special characters | - | minus sign (hyphen) | -- the glyph printed in the Character column is the hyphen-minus (U+002D), the same width as the crossbar of the '+' glyph printed directly above it, and the Meaning column names it '(hyphen)'.
claim.markdown_says: | | – | minus sign (hyphen) |   (specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 5111; the Character cell holds U+2013 EN DASH, confirmed by codepoint dump)
claim.why_it_matters: Table 1 is the normative enumeration of the COBOL character repertoire - the definitive list of which characters a conforming implementation must accept in source. Transcribing the basic special character as U+2013 EN DASH puts a character that is NOT in the repertoire into the normative list and drops the one that is. Anything derived mechanically from this table (a lexer character class, a reserved-symbol table, a repertoire conformance test) would accept EN DASH as the minus/hyphen and reject the actual hyphen-minus, which is also the hyphen permitted inside COBOL words per 8.3.2.1. The Meaning column's own words '(hyphen)' contradict the transcribed character, so the markdown is internally inconsistent as well.

verdict.reasoning:
REFUTED by direct measurement of the canonical PDF. The claim's factual premise -- that the glyph printed in Table 1's Character column is the hyphen-minus U+002D -- is false, and the markdown's U+2013 is an exact transcription of what the PDF contains.

(1) GLYPH ADVANCE WIDTHS FROM THE PDF ITSELF. The page-121 text layer is codepoint-obfuscated (the extracted 'characters' are garbage: 'Ϊ', 'Ȃ', 'ȗ', ...), but the per-character bounding boxes are real geometry. All eight Character-column glyphs are set in Cambria at 10.70 pt. Their advances, divided by the 10.70 pt em, against Cambria's true advances (measured from C:/Windows/Fonts/cambria.ttc): '+' 5.927pt = 0.5540 em vs Cambria plus 0.5540; DASH 5.350pt = 0.5000 em; '*' 4.569pt = 0.4270 vs asterisk 0.4270; '/' 5.243pt = 0.4900 vs slash 0.4900; '=' 5.927pt = 0.5540 vs equals 0.5540; '$' 5.414pt = 0.5060 vs dollar 0.5060; ',' 2.193pt = 0.2050 vs comma 0.2050; ';' 2.825pt = 0.2640 vs semicolon 0.2640. Every advance matches Cambria to four decimal places, so the calibration is exact. In Cambria: hyphen-minus U+002D = 0.3320 em, EN DASH U+2013 = 0.5000 em, MINUS SIGN U+2212 = 0.5540 em, FIGURE DASH U+2012 = 0.5440 em, EM DASH = 1.0000 em. The printed glyph's 0.5000 em identifies it as U+2013 EN DASH uniquely and unambiguously. Had it been the hyphen-minus the claim asserts, the advance would have been 3.552 pt, not 5.350 pt.

(2) INDEPENDENT PIXEL CONFIRMATION AT 300 DPI. A connected-component sweep of spec_p121.png found every short horizontal bar on the page. The Table 1 dash has 18 px of ink (bbox x 1138-1155, y 674-676). The genuine hyphens on the same page are 9-10 px: the two U+002D hyphens in 'user-defined' inside the Extended letters cell of the very same table are 10 px (x 1777 y 1647; x 1778 y 1752), and the body-text hyphens plus the '--' pair in NOTE 1 are 9 px. The Table 1 dash is therefore very nearly twice the width of the hyphen printed two inches below it in the same table and the same font. Cambria rendered at the page's em size gives hyphen 11 px, en dash 19 px, minus 19 px, plus 19x19, equals 19x12, underscore 17 -- and the page measures plus 19x19, equals bars 19 px each spanning 12 px total, underscore 16 px. The rasterized evidence corroborates the advance-width evidence: the glyph is a half-em dash, not a hyphen.

(3) THE CLAIM MISQUOTES THE PDF ON ITS OWN KEY DETAIL. It asserts the dash is 'the same width as the crossbar of the + glyph printed directly above it'. The dash advance is 0.5000 em; the plus advance is 0.5540 em. Same-width would have meant U+2212 MINUS SIGN, which is what a 0.5540 em dash would have been -- and it is not that either. The claim reads its own conclusion out of a width it did not measure.

(4) THE 'INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY' ARGUMENT ALSO FAILS. 'minus sign (hyphen)' is ISO's own wording, printed verbatim in the PDF, because the single repertoire character fills both roles in COBOL: the arithmetic/unary minus and the hyphen permitted inside COBOL words. The parenthetical names the second role; it is not a caption of the glyph's Unicode identity. Per 8.1.3.1 ('The implementor maps the COBOL character repertoire to one or more coded character sets') and 8.1.3.2 GR 1 ('The implementor shall define a mapping of each basic letter, basic digit, basic special character ... to one or more coded character sets'), Table 1 enumerates SYMBOLS and assigns no codepoints at all; the mapping to a coded character set is implementor-defined. The 'space' row is decisive corroboration -- its Character cell is deliberately BLANK in the PDF (there is no glyph to print), and the markdown reproduces it blank. A column that can be empty is a column of illustrative symbols, not of normative codepoints. Nothing may be mechanically lifted from it as a lexer character class regardless of the transcription; the claimed downstream harm is not caused by the markdown.

CONCLUSION: there is no PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy here. specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 5111 holds U+2013 and the canonical PDF holds U+2013. This is not a transcription defect and does not belong in the reconciliation ledger. If anything is worth recording it is an observation about ISO's own typography (ISO depicts the minus/hyphen repertoire symbol with an en dash), which is a property of the canonical source, identical in both artefacts -- and which changes nothing normatively, since Table 1 binds no codepoints.
verdict.corrected_description: No discrepancy. The canonical PDF's Table 1 Character cell contains U+2013 EN DASH (advance 5.350 pt at a 10.70 pt Cambria em = 0.5000 em, matching Cambria's en dash exactly; hyphen-minus would be 0.3320 em / 3.552 pt and minus sign 0.5540 em / 5.928 pt), and specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 5111 transcribes it as U+2013. The markdown is faithful. The claim misidentifies the printed glyph and misstates its width relative to the '+' above it.
